Reviewer #1:

This submission is a revised version of a previous submission. The authors have done a substantial amount of work, and the paper has increased in length. Some aspects have greatly improved, such as the characterization of the roles of the cell wall, tension and actin (using drugs and mutants to change actin organization) in controlling endocytosis. The role of eisosomes in buffering membrane tension has been characterized in further details, providing the first evidence that eisosomes could play a similar role in yeast than caveolae in cells in buffering membrane tension. Finally, the authors added a study on the evolution of exocytosis during hypoosmotic shocks, which reacts in opposite direction than endocytosis.

While I value the efforts and work provided by the authors in their revised version, they in fact took an opposite direction in their revised manuscript than what was initially suggested by the reviewers: – split the manuscript in two, and strengthen the characterization of tension/endocytosis on the one hand, and eisosomes/tension on the other. Instead, the authors kept the two parts in the same manuscript, and added a third part on exocytosis. They also extended their comparison of walled cells and protoplasts, which is indeed interesting, but makes the flow hard to follow because the reader needs to go back-and-forth between different figures. This choice is at the expense of the manuscript's readability, which became lengthy and difficult to follow.

While I value the efforts made by the authors, and the improvement of the characterization of endocytosis, tension and eisosomes, I am embarrassed to say that the main criticism remains. I understand that the authors wanted to broaden their study, and get more general conclusions, but it does not go through well. I unfortunately cannot recommend publication in the present form, and would certainly suggest again to split the manuscript in two (which could be back-to-back in ELife for example), one on endocytosis/exocytosis and tension (where pil1delta and protoplasts would be used as a tool to dysregulate tension) and one on eisosomes/tension buffering.

– While the mechanism at play to regulate dynamics of endocytosis and eisosomes during osmotic shock became well characterized, the new part on exocytosis is very short and does not provide any further understanding of the regulation at play here. Is it tethering, or SNARE function that is regulated by tension? Is that higher tension strengthens the actin dome around exocytic vesicles to trigger fusion? A better characterization, at least at the same level of other parts would be needed here.

– Some plots are difficult to read. The plot "Speed" vs "time", which zero the invagination time, is not easy to read. The total duration of endocytic events is changing with conditions, and if I understood well, that is the main effect that the author look at, but it took me quite some time to figure out how to read these. I think a classic plot with average duration would be easier to follow for most readers. I understand that in some cases, the authors see no invagination, which is also reported in this graph, but I think 2 plots would do a better job than a single one in this case. Or perhaps, explain better how to read those plots, as they are uncommon, and at the basis of the authors' argumentation.

– I disagree with the use of deltaP to account for a change of osmolarity. Pressure should be in Pa (or any corresponding unit), not in Moles per Liter. Either the authors use deltaC, or they measure the osmotic pressure of their solution and can use Osm in this case for pressure. Also, at concentrations about 0.5M, there is usually a substantial discrepancy between Osmolarity and Molarity, and as the authors are using Molarities above 1M, I think it would be safer to estimate the osmotic pressure of those solutions.

Reviewer #2:

Lemiere and colleagues show in this manuscript that endocytosis is remarkably robust against osmotic changes in normal walled yeast cells. However, in cells without cell walls endocytosis is much more sensitive to osmotic changes, presumably due to changing membrane tension. Eisosomes are shown to be important for regulating membrane tension after osmotic shocks.

Changes in turgor pressure are also shown to transiently affect the frequency of endocytic events. Eisosomes are shown to be important for restoring the normal endocytic frequency after shocks. Finally, exocytosis is suggested to be a mechanism that restores normal membrane tension after hypotonic shocks.

The strength of the manuscript is the highly quantitative and careful experimentation and the fact that three different plasma membrane processes are considered together (endocytosis, exocytosis, eisosomes), which is surprisingly rarely done, even though they must be functionally connected.

I have some suggestions for the authors to improve their manuscript:

Lines 217-223: Does the plasma membrane area remain constant after hypotonic treatment? I.e. are the eisosomes really disassembled and not just diluted if the plasma membrane area increases?

Figure 4H: Looking at the time series images it seems like the plane of focus shifts during the experiment. At time zero, and at 1 minute, the focus is at the surface of the cell, but later it appears that the focus shifts toward the center of the cell. During the second half of the time series the remaining eisosomes are seen at the periphery of the cell, which could be explained by a focus shift. Is this a representative example?

Lines 325 : The authors could clarify a bit more clearly whether they quantify the density of endocytic events, or the density of Fim1 labeled endocytic sites, which would depend on the lifetime of the Fim1 patches. In other words, is the reported value the number of endocytic vesicles formed per area?

Line 340: I don't understand why the authors say that "volume increased faster than the change in endocytic density". Aren't they both significantly changed already at time 0, and it takes longer for the volume to reach maximum change?

Lines 379-382: This is the only place where potential non-vesicular mechanisms are brought up. Lipid transfer, for example, via membrane contact sites is a possible mechanism for expanding the plasma membrane area. The method used cannot distinguish between such non-vesicular transport and exocytosis. Therefore, the authors should bring this caveat up also in the discussion.

Lines 370-382: I think that the exocytosis assay is not totally intuitive. It might be useful for the readers if the authors tried to clarify the explanation a bit. In other words: how is it measuring exocytosis and not endocytosis, which FM4-64 is usually used to measure?

Line 520: How do the authors arrive at the value of 2%. Please elaborate.

Line 583: What is "higher order eukaryote"? (I would also advise against using "higher eukaryote", which, although commonly used, is not a clearly defined term, nor really biologically meaningful.)

results.result: Eisosomes disassemble in response to hypotonic shock and buffer membrane tension changes in protoplasts. At steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol, eisosomes in protoplasts are similar to walled cells with equivalent Pil1p concentrations. However, eisosome coverage decreases with decreasing osmolarity and correlates with cell volume. After hypotonic shock (ΔC = -0.2 M), eisosomes rapidly disassemble to ~50% coverage within 5 min. Micropipette aspiration shows membrane tension increases 1.6-fold in wild-type protoplasts (0.73 ± 0.21 mN·m⁻¹) but 4.5-fold in pil1Δ protoplasts (1.74 ± 0.61 mN·m⁻¹) after shock, demonstrating eisosomes buffer membrane tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C35 provide converging evidence from microscopy (eisosome coverage), biochemistry (Pil1p quantification), and biophysics (membrane tension measurements) that eisosomes disassemble in response to hypotonic shock and buffer membrane tension. The micropipette aspiration data (C31-C34) directly demonstrate the buffering function by comparing wild-type and pil1Δ responses. The quantitative measurements are internally consistent and support the conclusion (C35).

results.result: Eisosomes protect cells from hypotonic shock-induced death, with differential effects in protoplasts versus walled cells. Wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts survive small shocks (ΔC = 0.05 M) equally, but pil1Δ protoplasts are more sensitive to moderate shocks (ΔC = 0.1 M). Both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells survive single large shocks (ΔC = -1.2 M), but repeated shocks cause ~10% mortality per shock in pil1Δ cells while wild-type cells remain viable.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C44 demonstrate eisosomes' protective role through survival assays under different shock conditions. The data show dose-dependent effects in protoplasts and cumulative effects in walled cells. The experimental design appropriately controls for shock magnitude and cell type, and the conclusions (C38, C39, C44) are well-supported by the survival data.

results.result: Endocytic density decreases transiently after hypotonic shock, with recovery within 2-6 minutes. In wild-type protoplasts, volume increases up to 50% and endocytic density decreases up to 36% (ΔC = -0.2 M), while pil1Δ protoplasts show 20% volume increase and up to 79% endocytic density decrease (ΔC = -0.1 M). Walled cells show similar but faster responses (recovery <2 min). At steady state, wild-type cells maintain constant endocytic density across osmolarities (0-2 M), while pil1Δ cells show 56% increase at 2 M sorbitol.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C60 provide comprehensive quantitative data on endocytic density changes using a validated ratiometric method. The data show consistent dose-dependent responses across cell types and conditions. The temporal dynamics are well-characterized, and the conclusions about eisosomes' role in maintaining constant endocytic density (C57, C60) are supported by comparing wild-type and pil1Δ phenotypes.

results.result: Exocytosis rate increases after hypotonic shock in protoplasts but not in walled cells. Wild-type walled cells exocytose 4.6% of plasma membrane per minute at steady state. In protoplasts, wild-type cells show 41% increase in exocytosis rate after ΔC = -0.2 M shock (from 4.4 ± 0.2% to 6.2 ± 0.4% min⁻¹), while pil1Δ protoplasts show modest increase after ΔC = -0.05 M shock. Walled cells show minimal exocytosis rate changes even after ΔC = -1.2 M shock.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C71 use FM4-64 staining to quantify exocytosis rates across conditions. The method is appropriate and the data show clear differences between protoplasts and walled cells, and between wild-type and pil1Δ. The conclusion that eisosomes regulate exocytosis rate (C71) is supported by the differential responses. However, the authors acknowledge that FM4-64 uptake could reflect non-exocytic lipid transfer mechanisms, which is not fully addressed.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition experiments support the roles of endocytosis and exocytosis in membrane tension regulation. Blocking exocytosis with BFA increases protoplast death after hypotonic shock, while blocking endocytosis with LatA increases resistance starting 4 min post-shock but decreases resistance in the initial 2 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 support the hypothesis that modulating endocytosis/exocytosis affects survival, but C74 presents a contradictory result for LatA in the first 2 min. The authors acknowledge this contradiction but suggest LatA may have unidentified effects on protoplast survival or indirectly affect exocytosis. The interpretation is complicated by LatA's effects on all actin structures, not just endocytic actin. Additional controls or more specific inhibitors would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Actin dynamics during CME in walled cells is robust across chronic osmolarity changes but shows sensitivity in pil1Δ cells. Wild-type walled cells show no significant differences in fimbrin dynamics across 0-1.2 M sorbitol at steady state. After acute hypotonic shock (ΔC = -1.2 M), wild-type cells show ~15% faster fimbrin assembly/disassembly but unchanged peak numbers. In contrast, pil1Δ cells recruit 10-17% fewer fimbrin molecules at high osmolarities and show 30% increase in peak fimbrin with 30% shorter timing within 2 min of shock, stabilizing by 4 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C86 use quantitative microscopy with temporal super-resolution to characterize actin dynamics. The data demonstrate wild-type cells' robustness (C76) and pil1Δ cells' sensitivity (C86) to osmotic changes. The measurements are internally consistent and the improved methodology (C75) provides high reproducibility. The conclusion that eisosomes regulate membrane tension at endocytic sites is well-supported by the differential responses.

results.result: Protoplasts can perform endocytosis under varying osmotic conditions, with actin machinery adapting independently of the cell wall. Wild-type protoplasts in 0.4-0.8 M sorbitol recruit similar fimbrin numbers as walled cells but with slightly longer timing. At 1.2 M sorbitol, timing is dramatically longer and endocytosis fails. At 0.25 M sorbitol, both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts perform endocytosis but require more Fim1p. The similarity of dynamics in protoplasts at 0.4 M sorbitol to walled cells suggests this osmotic pressure (~1 MPa) approximates natural turgor pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 demonstrate that protoplasts can perform endocytosis across a range of osmolarities, supporting the conclusion that actin machinery adapts independently of the cell wall (C90). The inference about natural turgor pressure (C92) is reasonable given the similarity of dynamics and is supported by citation to previous measurements. The data are consistent across wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts.

results.result: The endocytic actin machinery rapidly adapts to acute increases in membrane tension. After low/medium shocks (ΔC = -0.05 to -0.1 M) in wild-type protoplasts, no stalled events occur and endocytosis completes successfully. After ΔC = -0.2 M shock, sites recruit 20% more fimbrin and take ~25% longer, but restore steady-state behavior within 4 min. In protoplasts pre-equilibrated at 0.25 M sorbitol (with fewer eisosomes), a ΔC = -0.1 M shock causes 73% more fimbrin accumulation and ~60% longer timing, similar to pil1Δ protoplasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 demonstrate the actin machinery's adaptive capacity using quantitative fimbrin dynamics measurements. The data show dose-dependent responses and temporal recovery. The comparison between wild-type protoplasts at 0.25 M (with disassembled eisosomes) and pil1Δ protoplasts (C97) provides strong evidence that eisosome structures, not just Pil1p protein, are responsible for the protective effect. The conclusions (C98, C99) are well-supported.

results.result: Membrane tension regulation involves three parallel mechanisms: cell wall mechanical protection, eisosome disassembly, and endocytosis/exocytosis balance. The cell wall provides the largest protection, as its removal dramatically affects actin dynamics and eisosome assembly. Surprisingly, endocytosis proceeds in protoplasts at osmolarities as low as 0.25 M where most eisosomes are disassembled. The actin machinery can overcome membrane tensions high enough to rupture the plasma membrane, as no stalled patches or comet tails were observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 synthesize the major findings into an integrated model. The evidence for parallel mechanisms (C101) comes from comparing responses across cell types (walled vs protoplasts, wild-type vs pil1Δ). The relative contributions are well-supported by the data. The observation that endocytosis proceeds at 0.25 M (C104) and the absence of stalled patches (C105) are important findings that distinguish this work from studies in S. cerevisiae.

results.result: The findings contrast with S. cerevisiae studies and add to evidence for eisosomes' critical role in membrane tension regulation. Unlike S. cerevisiae where endocytosis is blocked and actin comet tails form within 2 min of hypotonic shock, S. pombe maintains endocytosis. Eisosomes regulate membrane tension through dynamic remodeling and scaffolding, with membrane tension decreased via eisosome disassembly releasing excess surface area. Pil1p undergoes rapid exchange at eisosome ends, potentially enabling rapid disassembly. Disassembled eisosome components have altered phosphorylation or localization, potentially signaling to endocytosis/exocytosis pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111 place the findings in broader context and propose mechanisms. The contrast with S. cerevisiae (C106) is well-documented by citation. The conclusions about eisosomes' role (C108, C109) are supported by the current data and previous work. The mechanistic proposals about Pil1p exchange (C110) and signaling (C111) are supported by citations to previous work, though C111 is somewhat speculative about the signaling mechanisms.

results.result: Quantitative estimates show that modulating endocytosis and exocytosis rates can efficiently increase plasma membrane surface area, though more slowly than eisosome disassembly. Cells endocytose ~2% of surface area per minute through CME. In pil1Δ protoplasts after ΔC = -0.05 M shock, the net surface area added over 10 min (5% from reduced endocytosis + 6% from increased exocytosis = 11%) matches the measured ~12% surface area increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 provide quantitative estimates that integrate endocytosis and exocytosis measurements. The calculations are transparent and the agreement between predicted (11%) and measured (12%) surface area increase (C113) supports the model. The conclusion about relative time scales (C114) is reasonable given eisosome disassembly occurs within 5 min while endocytosis/exocytosis modulation requires 10 min.

results.result: Fission yeast CME is robust and can proceed across wide ranges of osmolarities and membrane tensions. Even cells lacking cell wall and eisosomes perform endocytosis after acute membrane tension changes if the plasma membrane remains intact. Under increased membrane tension/turgor pressure, the endocytic actin machinery assembles more fimbrin molecules and takes longer to produce vesicles, strongly supporting the idea that actin machinery provides force to counteract membrane tension and turgor pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 summarize key findings about CME robustness and actin's force-generating role. The data showing increased fimbrin assembly under high tension (C117) directly support the force-generation model (C118). The robustness claim (C115) is well-documented across multiple experimental conditions. The interpretation that increased actin assembly reflects increased force requirements is logical and well-supported.

results.result: Multiple hypotheses are proposed for how actin dynamics is regulated under varying membrane tension: (1) mechanical/geometrical regulation where actin assembles until membrane deformation/scission occurs; (2) enhanced activity/recruitment of proteins upstream of actin nucleators; (3) increased cytoplasmic protein concentration due to fewer endocytic sites. Evidence suggests 65-85% of endocytic proteins are at endocytic sites at any time. Early endocytic proteins sensitive to membrane tension may fail to bind plasma membrane or prevent actin assembly triggering when tension is high, consistent with mammalian cell studies showing increased stalled clathrin-coated pits under high tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 present multiple speculative hypotheses about molecular mechanisms. While the hypotheses are reasonable and supported by some evidence (C122, C124, C125), they remain largely untested in this study. The authors appropriately present these as hypotheses requiring further investigation. results.result: Background and motivation: Actin assembly is required for CME in eukaryotes to overcome membrane tension and turgor pressure, but molecular mechanisms of actin machinery adaptation to varying membrane tension remain unknown. Yeast cells have high turgor pressure (0.6 MPa for S. cerevisiae, >1 MPa for S. pombe), requiring thousands of pN for vesicle formation. The cell wall buffers pressure changes, and eisosomes may regulate membrane tension, but their role in intact cells and influence on CME is unclear. Fission yeast is an ideal model system due to high turgor pressure requiring actin for CME, lack of adhesion machinery/actin cortex, and available quantitative microscopy methods.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Cells rapidly reduce membrane tension using three parallel mechanisms - cell wall mechanical protection, eisosome disassembly (buffering moderate changes on minute time scale), and temporary shifts in endocytosis/exocytosis balance (2-6 min reduction in endocytosis, ≥5 min increase in exocytosis). The endocytic actin machinery rapidly adapts to perform CME after abrupt membrane tension increases.
